questions.title: How much iron did Song China produce in the eleventh century?
questions.evidence: A widely cited estimate puts Chinese iron production in 1078 at about 125,000 tons. It comes largely from Song government accounts that recorded what officials collected from iron producers. Turning receipts into total output requires knowing whether a figure was a quota, a tax payment or the production of a particular works. Published excavations provide checks for some places.
questions.method: Trace the major figures back to their entries, recording the unit, district and fiscal rule in force. Calculate output under each defensible interpretation and compare the results with independent local accounts or furnace evidence. Show which districts and assumptions drive the national estimate.

questions.title: How much American silver reached China between 1550 and 1800?
questions.evidence: Silver mined in the Americas reached China across the Pacific via Manila and by routes through Europe and Asia. Mint and treasury accounts record production and some shipments. Chinese markets also received Japanese silver, and merchants evaded customs. Adding up recorded arrivals can count the same metal several times as it changed ports.
questions.method: Reconstruct flows one route and decade at a time, pairing departures with receipts and converting local units into silver weight. Check whether the quantities attributed to China are compatible with production and recorded sales elsewhere. Show how estimates change under different allowances for unregistered trade.

questions.title: Which lost silent films survive in fragments whose titles are unknown?
questions.evidence: Archives hold fragments of silent films whose identifying titles have disappeared. Eye Filmmuseum makes some available to watch. Trade papers, copyright descriptions and publicity stills can identify a scene. A recent search matched one shipwreck sequence to The Adorable Savage, only to find that Eye had already identified it under another catalogue description.
questions.method: Record the sequence of actions, surviving words and unusual props before searching for a title. Use one detail to find candidates and another to test them against original footage. Check both the archive’s attribution history and surviving-print records before claiming a lost film has resurfaced.

questions.title: How many people were carried in the Indian Ocean slave trades, 1500–1850?
questions.evidence: Historians have reconstructed parts of the trade in enslaved people across the Indian Ocean, particularly voyages recorded by European companies. Dutch, Cape and some Portuguese and French records survive online. People also travelled in small groups aboard mixed cargo vessels or with local carriers whose records survive unevenly. The size of these gaps matters to any total.
questions.method: Link departures and arrivals using vessel, captain, date and ports. Distinguish repeated reports of the same passage from a later resale or onward voyage. Calculate documented minimums by route and decade, then test how far independent port records support an estimate for missing traffic.

questions.title: Were real wages in the Yangzi delta and Bengal comparable to England's before 1750?
questions.evidence: One argument about Europe’s industrial rise turns on whether workers in England could already buy more with their wages than workers in prosperous parts of China and India. Price lists survive, but wage quotations for the Yangzi delta and Bengal are scattered across accounts and regulations. Some rates included meals, and some were official allowances rather than payments.
questions.method: Match workers doing comparable jobs in the same decades and check what they actually received. Price a household’s food, fuel and cloth locally, allowing plausible substitutions. Test whether the difference persists across several account books and under different assumptions about the number of paid workdays.

questions.title: What language does Linear A record, and can any proposed family beat chance?
questions.evidence: Linear A survives mostly in short administrative records from Bronze Age Crete. Some signs resemble signs in the later Linear B script, which writes Greek. Borrowing their sound values produces possible pronunciations, but many proposed links to other languages depend on a handful of similar-sounding words. Sign images and searchable transcriptions are available.
questions.method: Specify the sound correspondences and recurring word endings that one proposed language would predict. Test them on inscriptions held back from the comparison, then repeat with unrelated languages and shuffled sound values. Check readings against photographs wherever changing one damaged sign would change the result.

questions.title: How did smallpox reach Aboriginal communities around Sydney in 1789?
questions.evidence: Smallpox devastated Aboriginal communities around Sydney in 1789, a year after the British colony was founded. Explanations include an introduction associated with the colony and a much longer route through northern Australia. Dutch records document smallpox at Makassar in 1782 and elsewhere in island Southeast Asia that decade. The intervening chain of cases is missing.
questions.method: Read dated Dutch reports alongside Sydney journals and early accounts from inland communities. Establish where each writer actually observed illness and when news reached the writer. An earlier outbreak overseas establishes a possibility. Connecting it to Sydney would require independent evidence along the proposed route.

questions.title: Did Europe’s three great medieval cattle plagues come from the east?
questions.evidence: Medieval chronicles describe widespread cattle deaths in Europe in 809–810, 937–942 and 1315–1325. Some writers specify cattle, others mention livestock in general, and some describe a severe winter. Digitized Latin, Irish and Arabic texts make it possible to compare reports from different places. Several chronicles can repeat one writer’s account and create the appearance of a much wider event.
questions.method: For each episode, trace reports back to their earliest witnesses and record the place, date range and animals named. Map the independent observations and check which regions had chroniclers reporting other livestock losses at the time. The first surviving mention can reflect record keeping as well as geography.

questions.title: Did Ptolemy observe the Almagest star catalogue or adapt Hipparchus's?
questions.evidence: Ptolemy listed positions for about a thousand stars in the second century CE. A systematic error in their longitudes has led scholars to ask whether he updated measurements made by Hipparchus some three centuries earlier. Only fragments of the earlier astronomer’s work survive. Modern catalogues let researchers calculate where stars appeared at either date.
questions.method: Compare the surviving ancient coordinates, then test competing explanations on the rest of the catalogue. Which errors would an observer in Ptolemy’s time make, and which would follow from shifting older measurements by a fixed amount? Allow for rounding and mistakes in later manuscript copies.

questions.title: When was the consonantal text of the Qurʾān standardized?
questions.evidence: Early Qurʾān manuscripts preserve a consonantal text to which readers supplied vowels. Tradition associates its standardization with the caliph ʿUthmān around 650 CE. Distinctive spellings shared across copies suggest a common written ancestor, but the surviving fragments cover different passages. Radiocarbon measurements date the animal skin, which could have been stored before use.
questions.method: Compare photographs of overlapping passages, recording rare shared spellings and corrections. Use independently dated manuscripts to test how early the common text must have circulated. Give separate weight to dates for parchment, dates for handwriting and later accounts of an official decision.

questions.title: What texts did Newton copy in the alchemical manuscripts whose sources are unidentified?
questions.evidence: Newton copied and commented on other writers’ alchemical work. Digital editions identify many of his sources and reproduce his manuscripts, but several passages remain unattributed. Authors borrowed from one another, and some works circulated under different titles or only in handwritten copies. Identifying a source would show what Newton had actually read.
questions.method: Start with a passage whose source editors have identified and test whether a search recovers it. Then search digitized texts for unusual sequences of words in the unattributed passages. Check candidate editions against Newton’s omissions, wording and copying errors, allowing for a translation or an intermediate manuscript.

questions.title: Who printed the anonymous and false-imprint books of eighteenth-century Britain?
questions.evidence: Many eighteenth-century British books name a distributor, give a fictitious place of publication or omit the printer entirely. Signed books from known presses offer comparisons. Digitized pages preserve decorative blocks and damaged letters that could leave a recognizable mark in different books. Some large scan collections require a subscription, and equipment could change hands.
questions.method: Begin with publicly accessible signed editions to test whether recurring chips or cracks identify particular blocks. Look for those details in anonymous editions and check dates against ownership of the press. Several independent matches can support an attribution. A common decorative design alone could belong to many printers.

questions.title: How did Gutenberg cast his type?
questions.evidence: Early printed letters that look identical to the eye show small differences when enlarged. Scholars disagree about whether these variations reveal how Gutenberg made his metal type. High-resolution images of early Mainz printing and several copies of the same Bible pages survive. Ink, paper, pressure and wear can all change the outline left by the same piece of type.
questions.method: Compare one letter in the same position across several copies of a page to measure variation introduced during printing. Then compare letters from different positions. Look for features that persist across impressions and check which proposed casting methods could produce the remaining differences.

questions.title: By what route did knowledge of gunpowder reach Latin Europe in the thirteenth century?
questions.evidence: Chinese texts attest knowledge of gunpowder by the eleventh century. Arabic and Latin references appear in the later thirteenth century, but the route connecting those written traditions remains unclear. Library records, digitized manuscripts and translations preserve names, marginal notes and sometimes a copyist’s date. An author’s purported lifetime can be much earlier than the surviving copy.
questions.method: Trace distinctive borrowed terms, named authorities and translation errors across dated witnesses. Look for an inventory, letter or ownership note placing a text with a particular intermediary before the Latin reference appeared. Shared terminology can support contact, but direction and timing need independent documentary evidence.

questions.title: How many people lived in China around 1600, and how many lives were lost to war, famine and disease between 1620 and 1680?
questions.evidence: Estimates for China around 1600 differ by tens of millions. Late Ming and early Qing officials counted taxable households and people under changing rules. Local gazetteers sometimes copied earlier figures decades later, even across war and displacement. Digitized local histories, tax returns and some genealogies allow comparisons below the national level.
questions.method: Follow the same counties across the change of dynasty. Compare population registers with genealogies and local accounts of deaths and flight. Estimate how much of the recorded decline could reflect migration, fewer births or missed households. Give ranges for the starting population and crisis deaths, with uncertainty for counties the sources scarcely cover.

questions.title: How many Indigenous people were enslaved in the Americas between 1492 and 1900?
questions.evidence: Estimates of Indigenous enslavement across the Americas rely on regional studies made from very different records. Sales, lawsuits over freedom, mission registers and estate inventories name some individuals. Where enslavement was restricted, documents could describe a captive as a servant or dependent. Digitized collections represent jurisdictions and centuries unevenly.
questions.method: Link named people and episodes within a region, checking each legal term in context and avoiding counting a resale as another person. Compare the resulting minimum with an independent series such as estate inventories. Show where the sources support an allowance for missing cases before combining regional ranges.

questions.title: Whose voices survive on unidentified early wax cylinders?
questions.evidence: Early wax cylinders preserve people whose names were never recorded or whose labels went astray. Public sound transfers sometimes contain spoken introductions. Programmes, recording catalogues and family papers can place a speaker at an event. Frederick Dent Grant has already been proposed for one Vienna recording, so the question there is how to confirm the identification.
questions.method: Transcribe names and distinctive phrases from the original transfer, then look for the same performance in dated programmes or a named recording. Have a listener check the words against the audio. A familiar-sounding voice or a later label copied from another catalogue offers limited independent support.

questions.title: Was rongorongo an independent invention of writing?
questions.evidence: Roughly two dozen surviving objects from Rapa Nui bear signs known as rongorongo. The inscriptions remain undeciphered. Photographs, transcriptions, three-dimensional scans of some tablets and published dates for their wood are available. Whether people carved the signs before European contact matters to the case for an independent invention of writing.
questions.method: Trace each object to its earliest documented appearance and compare repeated passages across tablets. Ask which clues date the carving itself. An old piece of wood could have been inscribed much later, and a regular sequence of signs alone does not establish that it encoded spoken words.

questions.title: When did Europeans first describe the outbreak later called syphilis?
questions.evidence: A severe outbreak Europeans called the French disease was widely recognized in the 1490s. Alleged earlier cases matter to the chronology on either side of Columbus’s return in 1493. Digital collections include medical tracts and contemporary chronicles. A writer recalling an earlier patient decades later could use a name learned only after the epidemic.
questions.method: Gather the earliest independent accounts and record separately when the illness occurred, when someone described it and when the surviving copy was made. Compare symptoms and the words contemporaries used with municipal orders from the same place. Distinguish the first recognizable description from a claim about the disease’s ultimate origin.

questions.title: In what year did the Zhou conquer the Shang?
questions.evidence: King Wu’s defeat of the Shang anchors early Chinese chronology. China’s national chronology project chose 1046 BCE, but the surviving sources give several plausible years. Bronze vessels bear calendar dates, later chronicles list reigns, and excavated material supplies radiocarbon ranges. The ancient terms for phases of the moon admit different readings.
questions.method: Use the inscribed dates to reconstruct calendars under each plausible reading. Check which also fit independent astronomical observations and radiocarbon ranges. If a proposed year works only with one disputed translation or one version of a chronicle, show how far the date moves when that evidence is set aside.

questions.title: Were Moses Shapira's Deuteronomy fragments an ancient text or an 1880s forgery?
questions.evidence: In 1883 Moses Shapira offered leather strips bearing a version of Deuteronomy for sale. Scholars pronounced them forgeries, and the strips subsequently disappeared. Surviving drawings, transcriptions, newspaper reproductions and Shapira’s papers have supported arguments on both sides. Without the originals, even the shape of a disputed letter can depend on who copied it.
questions.method: Compare independent witnesses line by line. For readings they agree on, check which spellings and letter forms were known to a possible forger in 1883 and which appeared in securely ancient finds only later. Flag conclusions that disappear when a different contemporary transcription is used.

questions.title: Why did plague disappear from western Europe after the early eighteenth century?
questions.evidence: After centuries of recurrent plague, western European cities experienced their last major epidemics at different times. Outbreaks continued around the Mediterranean after London’s last great epidemic in 1665, including in Provence in 1720. Port health registers, dated outbreak lists and quarantine correspondence survive unevenly. A city could escape because precautions worked or because its exposure changed.
questions.method: Pair ports with comparable trading connections and trace exposure over time using surviving arrival and health records. Compare the timing of epidemic decline with changes in trade, public health and local conditions. Include years when officials recorded threats but no local epidemic, and distinguish missing registers from quiet years.

questions.title: Where is leaf 170 of the Archimedes Palimpsest?
questions.evidence: A medieval scribe reused a manuscript of Archimedes for a prayer book. Several leaves later went missing. In Blois, a researcher identified leaf 123 by comparing it with a photograph taken in 1906. A photograph also survives for leaf 170. Finding the sheet could recover writing too faint to read in the old image.
questions.method: Trace sales and gifts through digitized catalogues and the available correspondence of former owner Anne Guersan. Look under descriptions of prayer books as well as mathematics. A candidate should match the photograph’s lines and distinctive damage, and a dated record should connect it to a present collection.

questions.title: Where was the land of Punt?
questions.evidence: Egyptian rulers sent expeditions to Punt for incense, gold and other goods. Temple reliefs show the people, cargo and ships, but give few directions. Published studies of Egyptian baboon mummies and imported stone narrow the possible sources of some goods around the southern Red Sea. A trading port could sell goods brought from inland or across the sea.
questions.method: Map the published places of origin for several kinds of cargo, keeping their dates separate. Compare the overlap with contemporary ports and excavated trade goods on both shores. An argument for Punt’s location must distinguish where Egyptians traded from where a particular animal or stone originated.

questions.title: When was Beowulf composed?
questions.evidence: Beowulf survives in one medieval manuscript copied around the year 1000. Its composition could have been much earlier. Verse rhythms, vocabulary and spellings have all been used to date it, but a scribe can modernize some features and preserve others. Manuscript images, early transcriptions and collections of other Old English poems are available for comparison.
questions.method: Test proposed signs of early composition on independently dated texts, particularly works that survive in later copies. Then examine whether the same signs agree across different parts of Beowulf. A method that mainly sorts texts by genre or by the date of the surviving copy cannot securely date the poem.

questions.title: How many early printed editions have no known surviving copy?
questions.evidence: European printers of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries issued books, pamphlets and single sheets that may survive in one copy or none. Catalogues, old inventories and fragments found in bookbindings offer glimpses of what disappeared. Cheap or heavily used works had different chances of survival from expensive volumes. The unit to count is an edition, however many copies it once had.
questions.method: Fit a model to a catalogue as it stood at an earlier date, then see how well it predicts editions discovered later, by format and genre. Compare its estimates with old inventories. Report how much the inferred total depends on publications that would be unlikely to leave even an inventory entry.

questions.title: Did the population of Ottoman Anatolia collapse in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries?
questions.evidence: Sixteenth-century Ottoman tax surveys suggest a growing population in Anatolia, followed by a marked decline in some records. Many early registers counted taxable household heads. Later registers could group several households into a single tax unit. Published registers and historical place-name lists make it possible to follow some villages across the change.
questions.method: Match settlements across successive registers, checking variant names and boundary changes. Where another local record counts actual households, use it to estimate how many lay behind one tax unit. Test whether the apparent fall persists within the same places under plausible conversions and after allowing for migration.

questions.title: What caused the cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576 in New Spain?
questions.evidence: Nahua and Spanish witnesses described devastating epidemics in New Spain in 1545 and 1576. The Nahuatl term cocoliztli could describe a severe pestilence with more than one cause. Published studies of epidemic burials in Oaxaca have identified evidence of enteric fever in some individuals. That finding leaves open the causes of deaths elsewhere and in the later outbreak.
questions.method: Separate the two epidemics and map the places, seasons and symptoms that independent witnesses report. Compare each account with the dates and locations covered by published burial studies. Distinguish a diagnosis supported at one site from an explanation that fits the wider pattern of deaths.

questions.title: Which old books preserve overlooked word lists from little-documented languages?
questions.evidence: Early travellers sometimes printed vocabulary lists in books with no mention of language in the title. For a language documented only rarely, one such page could preserve otherwise unknown words. A pilot catalogue covers 42 languages. It also shows how one traveller’s printed list could reappear decades later under another author’s name.
questions.method: Test a search on known lists in digitized travel books, then apply it to a defined collection of natural histories or voyage accounts. Check each discovery against the page image and earlier bibliographies. Shared errors, word order and translations can reveal which lists derive from the same encounter.

questions.title: Were Mendel's pea-hybrid data too close to expectation, and if so, why?
questions.evidence: Gregor Mendel published counts of pea plants that closely fit the ratios predicted by his account of inheritance. Ronald Fisher later argued that the overall fit was unusually good. The tables survive, but few working records show how ambiguous plants were classified, experiments repeated or results selected for publication. Different practices could produce similar totals.
questions.method: Reconstruct the sequence of experiments from Mendel’s paper and simulate the results of specific counting or reporting practices documented in contemporary sources. Test whether one explanation accounts for several features of the tables at once. Statistical fit can establish plausibility more readily than it can establish someone’s intent.

questions.title: How large was the Roman citizen population in the late Republic and under Augustus?
questions.evidence: A Roman census in 70/69 BCE recorded roughly 910,000 citizens. Augustus later reported over four million for 28 BCE. Scholars disagree over which people each total included, especially women and children. Resolving this would change estimates of Italy’s population. Inscriptions preserve the claims, and regional archaeological surveys offer independent evidence of settlement.
questions.method: Translate each interpretation into a population and an expected density of farms and towns in well-surveyed regions. Compare those predictions with dated sites, allowing for missed settlements and different survey techniques. Check whether the evidence can distinguish rival ways of counting citizens from actual population growth.

questions.title: Who could read and write in late imperial China, and how widespread were those skills?
questions.evidence: Estimates of literacy in Qing China have drawn on schooling, the market for primers and observers’ reports. Surviving contracts provide a different kind of evidence. Some parties signed in their own hand, others made a mark, and sometimes a scribe wrote everyone’s name. Selected collections of these documents can be read online.
questions.method: Sample contracts across regions and decades and check who signed in their own hand. Compare the results with evidence of schooling, reading and letter writing for the same groups. Report reading and writing separately where possible, and say which places, periods and people the surviving sources let us describe.

questions.title: Does the Indus script encode language, or a non-linguistic sign system?
questions.evidence: Seals and other objects from the Indus civilization carry strings averaging about five signs. Their order has patterns, but ownership marks and other systems can also have rules without spelling out speech. Photographs and sign-by-sign catalogues survive. There is no generally accepted bilingual inscription that gives the signs a reading.
questions.method: Test proposed ways to distinguish writing from other sign systems on examples whose function is known. Shorten those examples to the lengths found on Indus objects. Only a test that still distinguishes the known cases would make its verdict on the Indus signs informative.
