questions.title: Does Proto-Elamite record language, and is it the ancestor of Linear Elamite?
questions.evidence: Early Iranian accounting tablets preserve Proto-Elamite signs for numbers alongside signs whose meaning is less certain. Photographs and transcriptions record roughly 1,600–1,700 tablets. A sign beside a number could identify a commodity without spelling a word. Resemblances to the much later Linear Elamite script have also been proposed, across a long gap in the record.
questions.method: Group signs by where they occur in accounts and test that procedure on an early accounting system whose signs are better understood. Separately compare proposed correspondences across the two Iranian scripts. A claim of descent needs recurring matches in function and form beyond what chance resemblance would predict.

questions.title: Do khipus record more than numbers, and can their non-numerical signs be read?
questions.evidence: Andean record keepers tied knots in cords to represent numbers in a decimal system. Colour, the way threads were twisted and the arrangement of pendant cords may also identify people or categories. Public databases record these features, but few khipus can be securely linked to written accounts describing the same community or transaction.
questions.method: Start with well-documented pairs of cords and accounts. Propose what a repeated colour or construction feature marks, then predict its use in a different record before reading the associated account. Check whether totals or grouping alone explain the pattern. Reading a category would still leave broader claims about narrative open.

questions.title: Whose medical knowledge did Hans Sloane collect, and whose names survive in the record?
questions.evidence: Hans Sloane, a London physician, collected remedies and medicinal plants from around the world. His catalogues often name the person who delivered an item and say little about who explained its use. One lead concerns James Pawpaw, a Virginia healer. A printed account credits him with a remedy resembling one in an unsigned Sloane manuscript. Their relationship is still uncertain.
questions.method: Compare entries in Sloane’s plant catalogue with labels, letters and earlier accounts. Trace named and unnamed contributors across several cases to see whose expertise the catalogue preserved and where names fell out of the record. The Pawpaw manuscript offers one place to test how securely those connections can be made.

questions.title: Which women wrote the unsigned stories in nineteenth-century newspapers?
questions.evidence: Nineteenth-century newspapers reprinted stories across cities and countries, sometimes dropping a byline or substituting a pen name. Following an unsigned story back through digitized newspapers could restore work to a woman whose publications have been overlooked. Editors also shortened stories, and a syndicate could distribute the same mistaken attribution to many papers.
questions.method: Search distinctive phrases across reprints, then inspect the page image to make sure a byline belongs to the story. Seek a copyright registration, publisher’s payment or other independent link between the text, the name and the author. Check the method on stories whose authors are already documented.

questions.title: Which parts of Sumatra’s coast were struck by major tsunamis before instrumental records began?
questions.evidence: In Aceh, in northern Sumatra, coastal deposits and abandoned settlements point to tsunamis around 1394 and 1450. No contemporary written account of either wave has been identified. Farther south, a Dutch council dispatch describes repeated surges up the Padang River after an earthquake in 1697. It gives few clues about conditions elsewhere on the coast.
questions.method: Search regional and Chinese records for flooding at Acehnese ports under their historical names. For Padang, trace the damage survey mentioned in the dispatch and look for independent accounts from neighbouring ports. Compare the places and dates in those records with published coral and coastal evidence to establish how far each event can be traced.

questions.title: What did Nahua writers say about the people Spaniards described as having leprosy?
questions.evidence: In sixteenth-century Mexico, a friar used the Spanish word for leprosy in a festival description. Nahua writers described people whom dancers portrayed. The Digital Florentine Codex puts Nahuatl and Spanish accounts side by side, and early dictionaries record words for bodily conditions. A dictionary gloss, a ritual performance and an account of a sick person each answer different questions.
questions.method: Trace the Nahuatl terms and their spelling variants into independent accounts. Read who is speaking, whose body is described and how others responded. Compare the original wording with the Spanish translation before drawing conclusions about a shared diagnosis or people’s experience of illness.

questions.title: Which lost works of Galen survive unrecognised in Arabic and Syriac?
questions.evidence: Some works by the ancient physician Galen disappeared in Greek after translators had rendered them into Syriac or Arabic. Medieval scholars described their translations, and later authors sometimes quoted them. Digital manuscript images, searchable Arabic texts and a Greek–Arabic lexicon provide clues. A catalogue title can also conceal an abridgement or a different author.
questions.method: Search quotations for unusual phrases characteristic of a known translator and compare the surrounding argument with ancient descriptions of the lost work. Check the manuscript image and seek a second witness to the passage. A familiar medical opinion alone gives weak grounds for attributing it to Galen.

questions.title: When did the thylacine go extinct in the wild?
questions.evidence: The last known captive thylacine died in Hobart in 1936. Later reports from the Tasmanian bush range from detailed eyewitness accounts to newspaper stories repeated years afterwards. Bounty records, digitized newspapers and a published sightings database let researchers reconstruct some of those reports. The date of the last credible sighting and the date of extinction can differ.
questions.method: Trace late sightings to the earliest account, merging retellings of the same encounter. Test reliability criteria on older records from years when specimens independently confirm the animal’s presence. Estimate how the extinction range changes when doubtful reports are included and when fewer people were looking.

questions.title: Where was Agade, the capital of the Sargonic empire?
questions.evidence: Agade was the capital of Sargon’s empire in what is now Iraq. Ancient writers knew how to get there, but the rivers have changed course, and an inscription naming the city has yet to identify its site. Digitized tablets mention nearby towns, river crossings and stages of travel. Historical satellite photographs show abandoned channels.
questions.method: Map the routes described in texts of known date against river courses plausible for that period. See which candidate places satisfy journeys from several directions, including ones omitted when drawing the initial map. This could narrow the search even if identifying a particular mound ultimately requires excavation.

questions.title: How many people lived in the Americas in 1492?
questions.evidence: Estimates of the population of the Americas in 1492 differ by tens of millions. Most surviving tribute lists, parish registers and colonial inspections counted people after epidemics and displacement had begun. Published settlement surveys and radiocarbon dates offer a partly independent record of where people lived, with uneven coverage across regions.
questions.method: Reconstruct regions separately. Where early counts and archaeological surveys overlap, test the household sizes and rates of population loss needed to reconcile them. Carry those ranges into the hemispheric total and show which regions dominate the uncertainty. A well-documented valley can anchor its own estimate more securely than its neighbours’.

questions.title: Which of the journeys in Ibn Baṭṭūṭa's Riḥla did he actually make?
questions.evidence: Ibn Baṭṭūṭa dictated an account of decades of travel in the fourteenth century. Scholars have shown that parts of it borrow from earlier authors, including Ibn Jubayr. Searchable Arabic texts reveal some of those parallels, while independent records of the traveller himself are scarce. A visitor could borrow a description of a place he had actually seen.
questions.method: First test a passage-matching search on established borrowings. For disputed journeys, look separately for independently dated officials, ceremonies or encounters that place the traveller there. Record separately what the author borrowed and what evidence places him at the site.

questions.title: How much of the cacao along Amazonian rivers grew from colonial-era plantings?
questions.evidence: Cacao grew in Amazonia long before European colonization. Some groves along rivers today might descend from colonial plantings made for trade. A survey of the Rio Negro in 1774–75 names settlements and records production. Modern forest surveys record where cacao grows. Beans shipped from a village could have been harvested elsewhere.
questions.method: Separate the survey’s reports of planted trees from quantities of beans shipped. Locate the settlements on old and modern maps, then compare cacao abundance near documented plantings with similar floodplains elsewhere. Earlier Indigenous cultivation and natural differences between riverbanks could produce the same pattern.

questions.title: Did Kerala-school infinite series reach early modern Europe through Jesuit missionaries?
questions.evidence: Mathematicians in Kerala developed infinite series for quantities such as π before similar results appeared in seventeenth-century Europe. Jesuits worked in the region and corresponded with European mathematicians. A route for contact is plausible, but no known document records the transfer of those series. Access to manuscript correspondence and Indian mathematical texts varies.
questions.method: Search available letters, teaching notes and inventories for a recognizable worked example, diagram or sequence of terms. Date each witness and trace who could have read it before the European discoveries. Parallel mathematical results and travel between the two regions establish different parts of the case.

questions.title: How did potato blight first reach Europe in the 1840s?
questions.evidence: Potato blight appeared in European fields in the 1840s and helped precipitate the Irish famine. Agricultural letters describe early damaged crops, while shipping notices and customs records list consignments of potatoes. A port of departure says little about where a cargo was grown, and a newspaper’s publication date can postdate the first field damage.
questions.method: Work backwards from a named grower and a dated report of damage in West Flanders. Look for a purchase, delivery or consignment that can be traced to a particular Atlantic voyage. State where the documents actually connect the shipment to the farm and where the connection remains conjectural.

questions.title: Did the Black Death reach sub-Saharan Africa in the fourteenth century?
questions.evidence: The Black Death is documented in fourteenth-century Egypt and North Africa. Farther south, some excavated settlements were abandoned around this time, and surviving texts occasionally describe sudden mortality. Drought, conflict and migration can leave similar traces. Digitized chronicles, manuscript catalogues and published excavation reports cover some regions much better than others.
questions.method: Build local timelines from independently dated records and look for a contemporary account that can be placed at a specific affected site. Compare alternative explanations for abandonment. Where existing burial studies and written accounts cannot distinguish the cause, record how much of the question would require new physical evidence.

questions.title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura or other optical aids?
questions.evidence: A camera obscura projects a scene onto a surface. Some of Vermeer’s paintings show the soft focus and highlights such a device can produce. His household inventory lists no device. Museum images also show revisions beneath the paint and pinholes that a painter could have used to lay out perspective with string.
questions.method: Model the room in several paintings and predict where each technique would place edges, vanishing points and blurred details. Compare those predictions with museum scans, including paintings left out when building the model. A good visual imitation alone leaves open how Vermeer worked.

questions.title: Which volcano produced the sulfate deposit dated to around 1809?
questions.evidence: Sulfate in polar ice and eyewitness reports of a high haze point to a major eruption around 1809. The volcano remains unidentified. An 1836 account places an eruption of Lamongan in Java in December 1808, while the Latin work it cites describes November 1818. One copied date could create a false lead.
questions.method: Trace both dates back to their earliest witnesses and search surviving Dutch colonial correspondence for an independent, locally dated report of ash or darkness. Compare its timing with the haze observations. Identifying an eruption in Java would still leave the question of whether it produced the polar deposit.

questions.title: Did the age groups most at risk of dying change between waves of the “Russian flu”?
questions.evidence: The pandemic that began in 1889 returned in several waves. London medical reports and Danish burial records include ages at death, but the cities had different populations and used different age groups. A larger number of older people among the dead could reflect the city’s age structure or the season in which a wave arrived.
questions.method: Date the waves locally, match the age groups in death returns to those in the census, and calculate deaths above the usual seasonal level per resident. Compare successive waves within each city before checking whether the same shift in age-specific risk appears elsewhere.

questions.title: Do the missing voices of Renaissance songs survive in lute arrangements?
questions.evidence: Renaissance printers often sold each voice of a song in a separate book. A tenor book from a 1536 collection survives in Bern, but some companion parts are missing. Lute players arranged songs so that one instrument could play several voices. Digitized partbooks, lute music and contemporary catalogues allow comparisons even when titles have changed.
questions.method: Search lute arrangements for several distinctive phrases of the surviving tenor in the right order. Compare the full pieces, then check how the same arranger treated songs whose vocal parts all survive. An arrangement can recover a historical way to hear the piece while leaving particular lost notes uncertain.

questions.title: What do James Wilkinson's unread coded dispatches to Spanish officials say?
questions.evidence: James Wilkinson, a US Army officer secretly paid by Spain, exchanged letters in which numbers could give a word’s position in a dictionary. Some letters have words written above the code. Using published transcriptions, researchers recovered about three quarters of the words in one test letter. Several printings of John Entick’s dictionary have since been checked. Some reproduce the word order, but none examined puts the known words in all the right places.
questions.method: Group letters by coding system. Use some known words to test page and column positions in scanned dictionary editions, reserving others as a check. An edition that predicts those withheld words could then be tried on an unread passage and checked against a correspondent’s reply.

sources.label: Chu, Valenti and Knight’s study and dataset

questions.title: How common was sleeping in two shifts before industrialization?
questions.evidence: References to a “first sleep” helped establish the idea that people once routinely woke in the middle of the night before sleeping again. Digitized books, diaries and court testimony contain descriptions of nights, but a phrase can be figurative, translated or copied through many editions. A person awakened by a burglary tells us little about an ordinary night.
questions.method: Search for both interrupted and continuous nights, including descriptions that never use the phrase “first sleep.” Have readers classify independent accounts and distinguish exceptional events from repeated habits. Compare periods, occupations and kinds of writing before estimating how common the practice was.

questions.title: How many people did the Justinianic Plague kill, and did it change late antique society?
questions.evidence: Plague struck the Mediterranean world from the sixth century onward. Published evidence from burials identifies the disease, while eyewitness accounts describe heavy losses in particular cities. Neither establishes a death toll for the whole region. Tax documents on papyrus, inscriptions, excavated settlements and pollen records capture different aspects of life before and after outbreaks.
questions.method: Choose regions with continuous records and date their outbreaks independently. Compare changes in taxpayers, cultivated land and settlements with earlier trends and places affected by war or drought. Report where several sources agree and where a gap in record keeping prevents a mortality estimate.

sources.label: Published research on the first pandemic

questions.title: What missing passages of Hittite writing can we recover from broken clay tablets?
questions.evidence: Hittite scribes copied treaties, rituals and other texts onto clay tablets. Many survive in pieces. Searches of the TLHdig sign transcriptions can find plausible continuations, and splitting known texts into artificial fragments has helped test the method. Real pieces are damaged, photographs cover only part of the collection, and two tablets can preserve separate copies of the same passage.
questions.method: Search distinctive sign sequences on broken tablets and compare the results with photographs and published editions. A second copy can supply missing words. A physical join also requires compatible edges and line spacing. Show which lines can now be read and where a reconstruction is still uncertain.

questions.title: Is Jupiter’s Great Red Spot the same storm astronomers saw in the seventeenth century?
questions.evidence: A dark spot on Jupiter was recorded in the seventeenth century. Astronomers disagree about whether it survived to become the modern Great Red Spot. Paris drawings show a dark feature on three nights in 1714. It could be a different weather system. Digitized Paris and Marseille observing books preserve dated drawings and, sometimes, observations of Jupiter’s moons.
questions.method: Use the moons to check the time and orientation of each drawing. Compare the feature’s latitude and motion across nights and observing seasons. An empty drawing is informative only if the right side of Jupiter faced Earth and the observer drew features small enough to see the spot.

sources.label: Study of the Great Red Spot’s origin

questions.title: Can the Meroitic language be translated beyond its funerary formulae?
questions.evidence: Researchers can sound out the signs of Meroitic, a language of the ancient kingdom of Kush in northeast Africa. Familiar phrases on gravestones help identify names, family relationships and offerings. Royal and temple inscriptions are much harder to translate. Published photographs, transcriptions and museum records let readers compare words with the scenes and objects accompanying them.
questions.method: Build a small vocabulary and set of grammatical rules from the best-understood passages. Use them to predict the sense of a previously withheld inscription, then check the prediction against its setting and recurring expressions elsewhere. A translation should survive the loss of the picture that first suggested it.

questions.title: What is the absolute chronology of early second-millennium BCE Mesopotamia?
questions.evidence: King lists and dated business tablets establish the order of many events around the time of Hammurabi, yet rival chronologies put those events decades apart on our calendar. Copies of observations of Venus can fit several astronomical cycles. Excavated timbers and published radiocarbon dates provide a different clock, if they can be tied to particular reigns.
questions.method: Build a timeline from linked reigns and named years, then fit each proposed calendar to it. Check the dates it predicts against the published timbers and dated archaeological layers. Repeat with disputed readings of damaged tablets removed to see which calendar choices the evidence really distinguishes.

questions.title: What do the thousands of unread Shang oracle-bone graphs mean?
questions.evidence: Shang diviners recorded questions and outcomes on bones and turtle shells. Scholars can read many recurring signs, but thousands of distinct forms lack agreed readings. Photographs, ink rubbings and indexed inscriptions are available. A sign may occur only once or only in a personal name, and different hands can write the same word differently.
questions.method: Group uncertain signs by their appearance and by the words around them. Propose a reading using one group of inscriptions, then check whether it predicts the sense and grammatical position in previously withheld examples. Compare the original images before counting two drawings as separate evidence.

questions.title: Did Cassini see the star that exploded in Cassiopeia in the 1670s?
questions.evidence: The star whose remains are called Cassiopeia A exploded roughly three and a half centuries ago. A French report in June 1671 says the astronomer Cassini had seen stars missing from earlier counts of that constellation. His 1669 notebook survives, but his regular Paris journal starts after the report. Later entries mention Cassiopeia without identifying an explosion.
questions.method: Read the notebook and journals for dated sketches, measurements or named neighbouring stars. Reconstruct the sky for each date and check Cassini’s accuracy on stars we can identify. A description must distinguish the remnant’s position from other stars in the same constellation.

questions.title: How, if at all, did Copernicus learn of the Maragha-school planetary models?
questions.evidence: Copernicus used mathematical devices resembling those developed by astronomers at Maragha and elsewhere in the Islamic world. Surviving diagrams establish the resemblance. What remains unclear is how a particular idea might have reached him. Digitized Arabic, Greek and European manuscripts, library inventories and books he annotated preserve parts of the possible chain.
questions.method: Compare distinctive diagram labels and unusual errors across copies. For a promising match, trace the manuscript’s owners and dates against the movements of Copernicus and his teachers. A copy known to be in the right library at the right time is stronger evidence than two astronomers drawing the same geometry.

questions.title: What writings can we recover from the scattered manuscript fragments of Dunhuang?
questions.evidence: Fragments from Dunhuang, in western China, now sit in libraries thousands of miles apart. Scholars have already reunited pieces by matching their writing and torn edges. The International Dunhuang Programme makes images from different collections available together. Scribes often copied the same Buddhist passage, and some older photographs omit an edge or show only one side.
questions.method: Use repeated words or an unfinished line to find possible neighbours. Compare the tears, handwriting, spacing and reverse of each sheet against published joins. Transcribe the passage as it reads before and after the proposed join so a reader can see what has been recovered.

questions.title: How many people were killed in the Irish rising of 1641?
questions.evidence: Witnesses to the Irish rising of 1641 left thousands of depositions, now digitized. Some name people killed, others repeat reports about whole groups. Early polemical totals were much higher than modern estimates. The collection records deaths among Protestant settlers more fully than deaths among Catholics, and deaths in flight present a separate counting problem.
questions.method: Link names, places and dates across statements, recording who actually saw each death. Use a second reader to check uncertain matches and group counts. Give a documented minimum and plausible bounds, distinguishing violent deaths from later deaths through exposure and stating whose losses the records can represent.

questions.title: Where was Yamatai, the realm of Queen Himiko?
questions.evidence: A third-century Chinese account describes a journey to Queen Himiko’s realm in Japan. Following its directions and travel times literally takes a traveller offshore. Scholars have proposed centres in Kyushu and around Nara. Digitized excavation reports record settlements, tombs and imported objects from the period, but each candidate region has conspicuous finds.
questions.method: Map the routes permitted by different readings of the itinerary, recording every change of direction or unit assumed. Then test where each route predicts both a political centre and neighbouring settlements against independently dated excavations. A single impressive tomb could fit several accounts.

questions.title: Did Gregorian chant descend from Old Roman chant, or did both come from a common ancestor?
questions.evidence: Gregorian chant as transmitted in Frankish lands shares words and musical phrases with the tradition called Old Roman chant. Surviving Roman books with melodies are later than the earliest Frankish witnesses. A late copy could preserve an older way of singing. Digital manuscript images and chant indexes let the same pieces be compared across books.
questions.method: Align the melodies of chants with the same words and look for recurring changes in phrase endings or ornament. Test competing family trees on chants omitted when building them. Allow for singers passing music by ear as well as scribes copying it, since both can produce local variants.

originalQuestions.title: Where is leaf 170 of the Archimedes Palimpsest?
originalQuestions.evidence: A 1906 photograph records the missing leaf’s text, ruling and damage. Only part of the correspondence about its ownership is accessible online.

originalQuestions.title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura or other optical aids?
originalQuestions.evidence: Museum images, technical studies and a household inventory survive. Perspective geometry and focus effects have received competing explanations, and no document records Vermeer using an optical device.

originalQuestions.title: In what year did the Zhou conquer the Shang?
originalQuestions.evidence: Bronze inscriptions, king lists, astronomical references and published radiocarbon dates survive. Their implications depend on disputed calendar conventions and identifications of celestial events.

originalQuestions.title: Whose voices survive on unidentified early wax cylinders?
originalQuestions.evidence: Public cylinder transfers, discographies and family papers preserve audible and documentary clues. Frederick Dent Grant is already a candidate for one Vienna voice, with independent confirmation still open.

originalQuestions.title: Where was Yamatai, the realm of Queen Himiko?
originalQuestions.evidence: A Chinese account gives directions and travel times. Digitized Japanese site reports contain dated settlements, tombs and imported objects. Literal readings of the itinerary lead offshore.

originalQuestions.title: Which volcano produced the sulfate deposit dated to around 1809?
originalQuestions.evidence: Ice cores date the atmospheric event. An 1836 account places a Javanese eruption in December 1808, while the Latin source it cites gives November 1818.

originalQuestions.title: What do the thousands of unread Shang oracle-bone graphs mean?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digital collections include photographs, rubbings and indexed graphs from Shang divination records. Many unread signs occur rarely or only in names.

originalQuestions.title: Does the Indus script encode language, or a non-linguistic sign system?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digital corpora record signs and their order on seals and other objects. Inscriptions average about five signs, which makes comparisons with known writing systems difficult.

originalQuestions.title: How literate was the population of late imperial China?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized contracts preserve signatures, scribes’ handwriting and personal marks. Signing one’s name and reading prose reflect different abilities, and the contracting population was selective.

originalQuestions.title: How many people lived in the Americas in 1492?
originalQuestions.evidence: Tribute lists and missionary counts often begin after epidemics had already reduced populations. Archaeological settlement estimates cover different regions and dates.

originalQuestions.title: Where was the land of Punt?
originalQuestions.evidence: Egyptian reliefs depict expeditions and imported goods. Archaeological reports and published provenance studies place some imports regionally, although goods could travel through intermediate ports.

originalQuestions.title: Did Cassini see the star that exploded in Cassiopeia in the 1670s?
originalQuestions.evidence: A 1671 printed report mentions Cassini observing previously uncounted stars. His Paris observing journals survive online, but identifying one star requires enough positional detail.

originalQuestions.title: Did Ptolemy observe the Almagest star catalogue or adapt Hipparchus's?
originalQuestions.evidence: Ptolemy’s catalogue preserves coordinates for about 1,025 stars. Only fragments of Hipparchus’s earlier observations survive, while modern star positions can be calculated for both eras.

originalQuestions.title: How common was sleeping in two shifts before industrialization?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized books, diaries and court testimony describe waking from a “first sleep.” Printed examples include repeated quotations, translations and exceptional nights.

originalQuestions.title: When did the thylacine go extinct in the wild?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized Tasmanian newspapers, bounty records and graded sighting databases span different periods. Published extinction estimates change substantially with the reliability assigned to later sightings.

originalQuestions.title: When was the consonantal text of the Qurʾān standardized?
originalQuestions.evidence: Early Qurʾān fragments, photographs and published dating results cover several collections. Parchment dates can precede writing, and coverage of early variants is uneven.

originalQuestions.title: How many people did the Justinianic Plague kill, and did it change late antique society?
originalQuestions.evidence: Published burial studies identify plague. Digitized papyri, laws, inscriptions and pollen records cover different regions and give indirect evidence about deaths and social disruption.

originalQuestions.title: Which Atlantic shipments can be linked to Europe’s first potato blight outbreaks?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized agricultural letters, port reports and newspapers document shipments and early European outbreaks. Cargo origins, intermediate ports and deliveries to individual farms can be difficult to connect.

originalQuestions.title: Did the Black Death reach sub-Saharan Africa in the fourteenth century?
originalQuestions.evidence: Medieval accounts and published burial studies cover parts of Africa unevenly. Many settlements show abandonment without preserving evidence that identifies its cause.

originalQuestions.title: How much American silver reached China between 1550 and 1800?
originalQuestions.evidence: Treasury, mint and shipping records cover several routes at uneven intervals. Smuggling went unregistered, and Japanese silver also entered the Chinese market.

originalQuestions.title: What language does Linear A record, and can any proposed family beat chance?
originalQuestions.evidence: Searchable transcriptions and sign images survive for roughly 1,500 mostly short administrative documents. Proposed readings depend partly on sound values borrowed from Linear B.

originalQuestions.title: What do James Wilkinson's unread coded dispatches to Spanish officials say?
originalQuestions.evidence: Published code–word pairs and digitized dictionaries permit edition comparisons. Some letters have contemporary readings, while access to surviving originals varies.

originalQuestions.title: Did the age groups most at risk of dying change between waves of the “Russian flu”?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized London reports and Danish burial records preserve age-specific deaths during successive waves. Age brackets, population structure and recorded causes differ across cities.

originalQuestions.title: Do old drawings show Jupiter’s Great Red Spot between 1713 and 1831?
originalQuestions.evidence: Paris and Marseille observatory archives preserve dated drawings. Dark marks can represent different features, and the part of Jupiter visible changes as the planet rotates.

originalQuestions.title: Did anyone write down the Aceh tsunamis of c. 1394 and c. 1450?
originalQuestions.evidence: Coastal deposits and archaeology date two destructive waves. Searchable Ming court records and regional chronicles survive, with uneven geographic coverage and dating.

originalQuestions.title: How did a dodo become the subject of a Mughal painting?
originalQuestions.evidence: A 1615 ship’s journal records dodos taken on Mauritius. Peter Mundy later described live dodos in Surat. Neither record traces a particular bird to the Mughal painter.

originalQuestions.title: Where was Agade, the capital of the Sargonic empire?
originalQuestions.evidence: Cuneiform texts place Agade near other cities, and satellite images preserve ancient river courses. No inscription naming Agade has been found at its original site.

originalQuestions.title: Were real wages in the Yangzi delta and Bengal comparable to England's before 1750?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized grain prices, scattered wage quotations and company accounts survive. Occupations, payment in kind and the cost of comparable household goods vary across the three regions.

originalQuestions.title: What is the absolute chronology of early second-millennium BCE Mesopotamia?
originalQuestions.evidence: King lists, astronomical observations, tree rings and published radiocarbon dates supply chronological anchors. Several astronomical texts survive only in later, damaged copies.

originalQuestions.title: What texts did Newton copy in the alchemical manuscripts whose sources are unidentified?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digital editions transcribe Newton’s notebooks and identify many of his sources. Unattributed passages use wording and procedures that recur across multiple authors.

originalQuestions.title: How much of the cacao along Amazonian rivers grew from colonial-era plantings?
originalQuestions.evidence: A digitized 1774–75 Rio Negro survey names settlements. Forest plots record cacao abundance today. Beans shipped from a village could have grown elsewhere.

originalQuestions.title: How did smallpox reach Aboriginal communities around Sydney in 1789?
originalQuestions.evidence: Dutch company records document smallpox in the Indonesian archipelago in the 1780s. Sydney accounts describe the later outbreak. The intervening chronology remains incomplete.

originalQuestions.title: How, if at all, did Copernicus learn of the Maragha-school planetary models?
originalQuestions.evidence: Some Islamic, Byzantine and European astronomical manuscripts are digitized, as are books Copernicus annotated. The mathematical parallels are known. Their route of transmission remains uncertain.

originalQuestions.title: What caused the cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576 in New Spain?
originalQuestions.evidence: Nahua and Spanish accounts describe symptoms and deaths. Published findings from epidemic burials cover limited places and dates across the two outbreaks.

originalQuestions.title: Was rongorongo an independent invention of writing?
originalQuestions.evidence: Photographs and transcriptions survive for roughly two dozen inscribed Rapa Nui objects. The age of the wood can differ from the date of carving.

originalQuestions.title: Were Moses Shapira's Deuteronomy fragments an ancient text or an 1880s forgery?
originalQuestions.evidence: The leather strips disappeared after their nineteenth-century sale. Surviving transcriptions, sketches and reports differ in detail, and some relevant archival papers remain offline.

originalQuestions.title: Can the Meroitic language be translated beyond its funerary formulae?
originalQuestions.evidence: An online inscription repertory and museum images preserve texts from Kush. Many sound values are known, but long bilingual texts and well-understood non-funerary passages are scarce.

originalQuestions.title: Which lost works of Galen survive unrecognised in Arabic and Syriac?
originalQuestions.evidence: A ninth-century translator listed Galenic works known to him. Digital editions, quotations and manuscript images preserve possible witnesses, sometimes under other titles.

originalQuestions.title: How many people lived in China around 1600, and how many died between 1620 and 1680?
originalQuestions.evidence: Local gazetteers record taxes, land and households. Official Ming population totals often preserved old fiscal quotas, and local records survive unevenly through the wars.

originalQuestions.title: When was Beowulf composed?
originalQuestions.evidence: The sole manuscript was copied around 1000 and has been digitally imaged. Linguistic and metrical features can reflect both composition and later copying.

originalQuestions.title: How large was the Roman citizen population in the late Republic and under Augustus?
originalQuestions.evidence: Surviving texts give census totals with a fourfold jump under Augustus. Regional archaeological surveys provide settlement evidence, but differ in how they recorded small sites.

originalQuestions.title: Did Europe’s three great medieval cattle plagues come from the east?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digital Latin, Arabic and Irish chronicles record animal deaths. Some notices describe famine or weather damage, omit the location, or repeat an earlier account.

originalQuestions.title: Who supplied the medical knowledge that Hans Sloane's catalogues attribute to unnamed people?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized catalogues, specimen labels and correspondence often name the European intermediary. A single entry may combine knowledge from several unnamed suppliers.

originalQuestions.title: How many people were carried in the Indian Ocean slave trades, 1500–1850?
originalQuestions.evidence: Dutch company and Cape records document some voyages and transfers. Portuguese and French holdings are partly digitized, and local carriers left uneven records.

originalQuestions.title: How did Gutenberg cast his type?
originalQuestions.evidence: High-resolution copies of early Mainz printing show variation within a single letter. Inking, wear, pressure and photography can also change a letter’s appearance.

originalQuestions.title: Which of the journeys in Ibn Baṭṭūṭa's Riḥla did he actually make?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized Arabic texts contain passages the travel narrative shares with earlier authors. Independent records placing the traveller at a particular stop are much scarcer.

originalQuestions.title: Which earthquake sent waves up the Padang River in 1697?
originalQuestions.evidence: A digitized Dutch dispatch describes repeated surges at several places. Wave heights are uncertain, and the published coral evidence permits more than one rupture interpretation.

originalQuestions.title: Did Kerala-school infinite series reach early modern Europe through Jesuit missionaries?
originalQuestions.evidence: Kerala mathematical texts predate the European results. Jesuit correspondence survives in print, scans and undigitized volumes. The mathematical resemblance alone leaves transmission unresolved.

originalQuestions.title: Which lost silent films survive in fragments whose titles are unknown?
originalQuestions.evidence: Eye Filmmuseum footage, copyright synopses and the digitized trade press preserve clues. One apparent identification had already been published under a different catalogue description.

originalQuestions.title: How many Indigenous people were enslaved in the Americas between 1492 and 1900?
originalQuestions.evidence: Freedom suits, sales and mission records survive in partly digitized American and Iberian archives. Legal restrictions encouraged euphemisms, and record coverage varies sharply by region.

originalQuestions.title: Which cultivated toromiro trees descend from wild Rapa Nui collections?
originalQuestions.evidence: A herbarium voucher identifies a particular Melbourne garden bed. Accession and donor records are partly digitized, and some specimens have uncertain dates or identifications.

originalQuestions.title: What did Nahua writers say about the people Spaniards described as having leprosy?
originalQuestions.evidence: The Digital Florentine Codex places Nahuatl and Spanish passages side by side. Dictionaries, ritual descriptions and accounts of actual patients represent different kinds of evidence.

originalQuestions.title: Which old books preserve overlooked word lists from little-documented languages?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized travel books and natural histories contain word lists outside their titles or indexes. An existing catalogue covers 42 languages. Some later lists copy earlier publications.

originalQuestions.title: Did the population of Ottoman Anatolia collapse in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries?
originalQuestions.evidence: Surviving registers record taxable households and settlements. The types of tax register and the units counted changed during the period of apparent population decline.

originalQuestions.title: Do khipus record more than numbers, and can their non-numerical signs be read?
originalQuestions.evidence: Public databases describe knots, colours and cord structures. Few surviving examples can be paired securely with colonial documents recording the people or goods involved.

originalQuestions.title: Did James Pawpaw’s remedy enter Sloane’s collection without his name?
originalQuestions.evidence: A digitized 1736 printed recipe names Pawpaw. An anonymous Sloane manuscript shares ingredients and wording, while its route into the collection remains uncertain.

originalQuestions.title: When did Europeans first describe the outbreak later called syphilis?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized early printed accounts and manuscript catalogues preserve contemporary terms for the illness. Several apparently early cases were described decades afterward.

originalQuestions.title: Who grew and smoked cannabis on Ternate in 1676?
originalQuestions.evidence: Two digitized Dutch records document a February 1676 decision and proclamation on Ternate. They record officials’ intentions and give little evidence about growers or enforcement.

originalQuestions.title: How many early printed editions have been lost without trace?
originalQuestions.evidence: Early-print catalogues, inventories and newly identified fragments record successive discoveries. Cheap, ephemeral formats had different chances of survival and of being catalogued.

originalQuestions.title: Did Gregorian chant descend from Old Roman chant, or did both come from a common ancestor?
originalQuestions.evidence: The traditions share texts and melodies. Early Frankish books often give words alone, and the surviving Old Roman melodies were written down centuries later.

originalQuestions.title: How much iron did Song China produce in the eleventh century?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized fiscal compilations record iron receipts by locality. Collection rates are disputed, and published archaeological production evidence covers only some sites.

originalQuestions.title: How many people were killed in the Irish rising of 1641?
originalQuestions.evidence: Trinity College Dublin has digitized about 8,000 depositions. They include eyewitness reports, repeated hearsay and overlapping victim counts. Coverage of Catholic deaths differs.

originalQuestions.title: Are Borneo’s wild elephants native, or descendants of a royal gift?
originalQuestions.evidence: Searchable Dutch East India Company records mention elephants at Javanese courts, including imported animals. Their presence there leaves the proposed journey through Sulu to Borneo undocumented.

originalQuestions.title: Which manuscript fragments from Dunhuang fit back together?
originalQuestions.evidence: The International Dunhuang Programme brings together images from dispersed collections. Repeated passages occur in different copies, and image quality varies.

originalQuestions.title: Which Hittite tablet fragments belong to the same tablet or preserve the same text?
originalQuestions.evidence: TLHdig provides searchable sign transcriptions. Museum photographs cover only part of the corpus. Distinct tablets can preserve copies of the same passage.

originalQuestions.title: Were Mendel's pea-hybrid data too close to expectation, and if so, why?
originalQuestions.evidence: Mendel’s published counts can be reanalysed. Few working records survive to show how he classified ambiguous plants or chose which experiments to report.

originalQuestions.title: Do the missing voices of Renaissance songs survive in lute arrangements?
originalQuestions.evidence: A rediscovered tenor partbook is digitized in Bern. Catalogues and surviving lute arrangements offer comparisons, although arrangers could change individual vocal lines.

originalQuestions.title: By what route did knowledge of gunpowder reach Latin Europe in the thirteenth century?
originalQuestions.evidence: Chinese, Arabic and Latin texts survive from different dates. Some manuscripts are digitized, but the intermediate translations and contacts connecting the traditions remain uncertain.

originalQuestions.title: Why did plague disappear from western Europe after the early eighteenth century?
originalQuestions.evidence: Dated outbreak records and some port health records are online. Quarantine and exposure records survive unevenly, including across ports with different epidemic histories.

originalQuestions.title: Which women wrote the unsigned stories in nineteenth-century newspapers?
originalQuestions.evidence: Digitized newspapers preserve different printings of the same story, sometimes with a byline. Syndicated copies can repeat the same mistaken attribution.

originalQuestions.title: Does Proto-Elamite record language, and is it the ancestor of Linear Elamite?
originalQuestions.evidence: Images and transliterations cover a large collection of early Iranian accounting tablets. Numerical signs are understood more securely than the other signs or their later counterparts.

originalQuestions.title: Who printed the anonymous and false-imprint books of eighteenth-century Britain?
originalQuestions.evidence: Scanned books preserve distinctive damage to type and ornaments. Signed editions offer comparisons, although access to some large image collections requires a subscription.

expandedQuestions.title: Which women wrote the unsigned stories in nineteenth-century newspapers?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Nineteenth-century newspapers reprinted stories across cities and countries, sometimes dropping a byline or substituting a pen name. Following an unsigned story back through digitized newspapers could restore work to a woman whose publications have been overlooked. Editors also shortened stories, and a syndicate could distribute the same mistaken attribution to many papers.
expandedQuestions.method: Search distinctive phrases across reprints, then inspect the page image to make sure a byline belongs to the story. Seek a copyright registration, publisher’s payment or other independent link between the text, the name and the author. Check the method on stories whose authors are already documented.

expandedQuestions.title: Whose voices survive on unidentified early wax cylinders?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Early wax cylinders preserve people whose names were never recorded or whose labels went astray. Public sound transfers sometimes contain spoken introductions. Programmes, recording catalogues and family papers can place a speaker at an event. Frederick Dent Grant has already been proposed for one Vienna recording, so the question there is how to confirm the identification.
expandedQuestions.method: Transcribe names and distinctive phrases from the original transfer, then look for the same performance in dated programmes or a named recording. Have a listener check the words against the audio. A familiar-sounding voice or a later label copied from another catalogue offers limited independent support.

expandedQuestions.title: In what year did the Zhou conquer the Shang?
expandedQuestions.evidence: King Wu’s defeat of the Shang anchors early Chinese chronology. China’s national chronology project chose 1046 BCE, but the surviving sources give several plausible years. Bronze vessels bear calendar dates, later chronicles list reigns, and excavated material supplies radiocarbon ranges. The ancient terms for phases of the moon admit different readings.
expandedQuestions.method: Use the inscribed dates to reconstruct calendars under each plausible reading. Check which also fit independent astronomical observations and radiocarbon ranges. If a proposed year works only with one disputed translation or one version of a chronicle, show how far the date moves when that evidence is set aside.

expandedQuestions.title: Which of the journeys in Ibn Baṭṭūṭa's Riḥla did he actually make?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Ibn Baṭṭūṭa dictated an account of decades of travel in the fourteenth century. Scholars have shown that parts of it borrow from earlier authors, including Ibn Jubayr. Searchable Arabic texts reveal some of those parallels, while independent records of the traveller himself are scarce. A visitor could borrow a description of a place he had actually seen.
expandedQuestions.method: First test a passage-matching search on established borrowings. For disputed journeys, look separately for independently dated officials, ceremonies or encounters that place the traveller there. Record separately what the author borrowed and what evidence places him at the site.

expandedQuestions.title: Can the Meroitic language be translated beyond its funerary formulae?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Researchers can sound out the signs of Meroitic, a language of the ancient kingdom of Kush in northeast Africa. Familiar phrases on gravestones help identify names, family relationships and offerings. Royal and temple inscriptions are much harder to translate. Published photographs, transcriptions and museum records let readers compare words with the scenes and objects accompanying them.
expandedQuestions.method: Build a small vocabulary and set of grammatical rules from the best-understood passages. Use them to predict the sense of a previously withheld inscription, then check the prediction against its setting and recurring expressions elsewhere. A translation should survive the loss of the picture that first suggested it.

expandedQuestions.title: How much iron did Song China produce in the eleventh century?
expandedQuestions.evidence: A widely cited estimate puts Chinese iron production in 1078 at about 125,000 tons. It comes largely from Song government accounts that recorded what officials collected from iron producers. Turning receipts into total output requires knowing whether a figure was a quota, a tax payment or the production of a particular works. Published excavations provide checks for some places.
expandedQuestions.method: Trace the major figures back to their entries, recording the unit, district and fiscal rule in force. Calculate output under each defensible interpretation and compare the results with independent local accounts or furnace evidence. Show which districts and assumptions drive the national estimate.

expandedQuestions.title: What do James Wilkinson's unread coded dispatches to Spanish officials say?
expandedQuestions.evidence: James Wilkinson, a US Army officer secretly paid by Spain, exchanged letters in which numbers could give a word’s position in a dictionary. Some letters have words written above the code. Using published transcriptions, researchers recovered about three quarters of the words in one test letter. Several printings of John Entick’s dictionary have since been checked. Some reproduce the word order, but none examined puts the known words in all the right places.
expandedQuestions.method: Group letters by coding system. Use some known words to test page and column positions in scanned dictionary editions, reserving others as a check. An edition that predicts those withheld words could then be tried on an unread passage and checked against a correspondent’s reply.

sources.label: Chu, Valenti and Knight’s study and dataset

expandedQuestions.title: When was the consonantal text of the Qurʾān standardized?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Early Qurʾān manuscripts preserve a consonantal text to which readers supplied vowels. Tradition associates its standardization with the caliph ʿUthmān around 650 CE. Distinctive spellings shared across copies suggest a common written ancestor, but the surviving fragments cover different passages. Radiocarbon measurements date the animal skin, which could have been stored before use.
expandedQuestions.method: Compare photographs of overlapping passages, recording rare shared spellings and corrections. Use independently dated manuscripts to test how early the common text must have circulated. Give separate weight to dates for parchment, dates for handwriting and later accounts of an official decision.

expandedQuestions.title: Where was the land of Punt?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Egyptian rulers sent expeditions to Punt for incense, gold and other goods. Temple reliefs show the people, cargo and ships, but give few directions. Published studies of Egyptian baboon mummies and imported stone narrow the possible sources of some goods around the southern Red Sea. A trading port could sell goods brought from inland or across the sea.
expandedQuestions.method: Map the published places of origin for several kinds of cargo, keeping their dates separate. Compare the overlap with contemporary ports and excavated trade goods on both shores. An argument for Punt’s location must distinguish where Egyptians traded from where a particular animal or stone originated.

expandedQuestions.title: Which manuscript fragments from Dunhuang fit back together?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Fragments from Dunhuang, in western China, now sit in libraries thousands of miles apart. Scholars have already reunited pieces by matching their writing and torn edges. The International Dunhuang Programme makes images from different collections available together. Scribes often copied the same Buddhist passage, and some older photographs omit an edge or show only one side.
expandedQuestions.method: Use repeated words or the continuation of a line to find possible neighbours. Compare tears, handwriting, line spacing and the reverse of each sheet, then check published joins. A newly verified pair could restore a passage or identify the manuscript to which an isolated scrap belonged.

expandedQuestions.title: Who printed the anonymous and false-imprint books of eighteenth-century Britain?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Many eighteenth-century British books name a distributor, give a fictitious place of publication or omit the printer entirely. Signed books from known presses offer comparisons. Digitized pages preserve decorative blocks and damaged letters that could leave a recognizable mark in different books. Some large scan collections require a subscription, and equipment could change hands.
expandedQuestions.method: Begin with publicly accessible signed editions to test whether recurring chips or cracks identify particular blocks. Look for those details in anonymous editions and check dates against ownership of the press. Several independent matches can support an attribution. A common decorative design alone could belong to many printers.

expandedQuestions.title: Were real wages in the Yangzi delta and Bengal comparable to England's before 1750?
expandedQuestions.evidence: One argument about Europe’s industrial rise turns on whether workers in England could already buy more with their wages than workers in prosperous parts of China and India. Price lists survive, but wage quotations for the Yangzi delta and Bengal are scattered across accounts and regulations. Some rates included meals, and some were official allowances rather than payments.
expandedQuestions.method: Match workers doing comparable jobs in the same decades and check what they actually received. Price a household’s food, fuel and cloth locally, allowing plausible substitutions. Test whether the difference persists across several account books and under different assumptions about the number of paid workdays.

expandedQuestions.title: How many people were killed in the Irish rising of 1641?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Witnesses to the Irish rising of 1641 left thousands of depositions, now digitized. Some name people killed, others repeat reports about whole groups. Early polemical totals were much higher than modern estimates. The collection records deaths among Protestant settlers more fully than deaths among Catholics, and deaths in flight present a separate counting problem.
expandedQuestions.method: Link names, places and dates across statements, recording who actually saw each death. Use a second reader to check uncertain matches and group counts. Give a documented minimum and plausible bounds, distinguishing violent deaths from later deaths through exposure and stating whose losses the records can represent.

expandedQuestions.title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura or other optical aids?
expandedQuestions.evidence: A camera obscura projects a scene onto a surface. Some of Vermeer’s paintings show the soft focus and highlights such a device can produce. His household inventory lists no device. Museum images also show revisions beneath the paint and pinholes that a painter could have used to lay out perspective with string.
expandedQuestions.method: Model the room in several paintings and predict where each technique would place edges, vanishing points and blurred details. Compare those predictions with museum scans, including paintings left out when building the model. A good visual imitation alone leaves open how Vermeer worked.

expandedQuestions.title: Did anyone write down the Aceh tsunamis of c. 1394 and c. 1450?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Coastal deposits and ruined settlements show that large waves struck the coast of Aceh in northern Sumatra around 1394 and 1450. The trading port of Lamri had contacts across the Indian Ocean and with China. A contemporary written account could connect the physical destruction with what happened to the people and the port.
expandedQuestions.method: Search the Ming court records and regional chronicles under the port’s different names, allowing a few years either side of each geological date. Check promising passages in the original language. A description of the sea entering a named settlement carries much more weight than a gap in tribute missions.

expandedQuestions.title: Where is leaf 170 of the Archimedes Palimpsest?
expandedQuestions.evidence: A medieval scribe reused a manuscript of Archimedes for a prayer book. Several leaves later went missing. In Blois, a researcher identified leaf 123 by comparing it with a photograph taken in 1906. A photograph also survives for leaf 170. Finding the sheet could recover writing too faint to read in the old image.
expandedQuestions.method: Trace sales and gifts through digitized catalogues and the available correspondence of former owner Anne Guersan. Look under descriptions of prayer books as well as mathematics. A candidate should match the photograph’s lines and distinctive damage, and a dated record should connect it to a present collection.

expandedQuestions.title: Who grew and smoked cannabis on Ternate in 1676?
expandedQuestions.evidence: In February 1676 Dutch officials on Ternate, an island in the spice-producing Moluccas, ordered the destruction of a plant they called gingie. A council decision and a public proclamation survive in digitized records. They show what officials intended. They say much less about who owned the gardens, who smoked the plant or what happened after the order.
expandedQuestions.method: Follow the officials, named places and variant spellings through later council minutes, petitions and correspondence. Look for a dated inspection, complaint or dispute involving growers. Compare the language of enforcement with the original proclamation to distinguish a reported action from another copy of the same order.

expandedQuestions.title: How many early printed editions have been lost without trace?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Early printers issued books, pamphlets and single sheets that may survive in one copy or none. Catalogues, old inventories and fragments found in bookbindings offer glimpses of what disappeared. Cheap or heavily used works had different chances of survival from expensive volumes. The unit to count is an edition, however many copies it once had.
expandedQuestions.method: Fit a model to a catalogue as it stood at an earlier date, then see how well it predicts editions discovered later, by format and genre. Compare its estimates with old inventories. Report how much the inferred total depends on publications that would be unlikely to leave even an inventory entry.

expandedQuestions.title: Did Gregorian chant descend from Old Roman chant, or did both come from a common ancestor?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Gregorian chant as transmitted in Frankish lands shares words and musical phrases with the tradition called Old Roman chant. Surviving Roman books with melodies are later than the earliest Frankish witnesses. A late copy could preserve an older way of singing. Digital manuscript images and chant indexes let the same pieces be compared across books.
expandedQuestions.method: Align the melodies of chants with the same words and look for recurring changes in phrase endings or ornament. Test competing family trees on chants omitted when building them. Allow for singers passing music by ear as well as scribes copying it, since both can produce local variants.

expandedQuestions.title: Did the Black Death reach sub-Saharan Africa in the fourteenth century?
expandedQuestions.evidence: The Black Death is documented in fourteenth-century Egypt and North Africa. Farther south, some excavated settlements were abandoned around this time, and surviving texts occasionally describe sudden mortality. Drought, conflict and migration can leave similar traces. Digitized chronicles, manuscript catalogues and published excavation reports cover some regions much better than others.
expandedQuestions.method: Build local timelines from independently dated records and look for a contemporary account that can be placed at a specific affected site. Compare alternative explanations for abandonment. Where existing burial studies and written accounts cannot distinguish the cause, record how much of the question would require new physical evidence.

expandedQuestions.title: What language does Linear A record, and can any proposed family beat chance?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Linear A survives mostly in short administrative records from Bronze Age Crete. Some signs resemble signs in the later Linear B script, which writes Greek. Borrowing their sound values produces possible pronunciations, but many proposed links to other languages depend on a handful of similar-sounding words. Sign images and searchable transcriptions are available.
expandedQuestions.method: Specify the sound correspondences and recurring word endings that one proposed language would predict. Test them on inscriptions held back from the comparison, then repeat with unrelated languages and shuffled sound values. Check readings against photographs wherever changing one damaged sign would change the result.

expandedQuestions.title: What is the absolute chronology of early second-millennium BCE Mesopotamia?
expandedQuestions.evidence: King lists and dated business tablets establish the order of many events around the time of Hammurabi, yet rival chronologies put those events decades apart on our calendar. Copies of observations of Venus can fit several astronomical cycles. Excavated timbers and published radiocarbon dates provide a different clock, if they can be tied to particular reigns.
expandedQuestions.method: Build a timeline from linked reigns and named years, then fit each proposed calendar to it. Check the dates it predicts against the published timbers and dated archaeological layers. Repeat with disputed readings of damaged tablets removed to see which calendar choices the evidence really distinguishes.

expandedQuestions.title: How large was the Roman citizen population in the late Republic and under Augustus?
expandedQuestions.evidence: A Roman census in 70/69 BCE recorded roughly 910,000 citizens. Augustus later reported over four million for 28 BCE. Scholars disagree over which people each total included, especially women and children. Resolving this would change estimates of Italy’s population. Inscriptions preserve the claims, and regional archaeological surveys offer independent evidence of settlement.
expandedQuestions.method: Translate each interpretation into a population and an expected density of farms and towns in well-surveyed regions. Compare those predictions with dated sites, allowing for missed settlements and different survey techniques. Check whether the evidence can distinguish rival ways of counting citizens from actual population growth.

expandedQuestions.title: How many people did the Justinianic Plague kill, and did it change late antique society?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Plague struck the Mediterranean world from the sixth century onward. Published evidence from burials identifies the disease, while eyewitness accounts describe heavy losses in particular cities. Neither establishes a death toll for the whole region. Tax documents on papyrus, inscriptions, excavated settlements and pollen records capture different aspects of life before and after outbreaks.
expandedQuestions.method: Choose regions with continuous records and date their outbreaks independently. Compare changes in taxpayers, cultivated land and settlements with earlier trends and places affected by war or drought. Report where several sources agree and where a gap in record keeping prevents a mortality estimate.

expandedQuestions.title: How many people lived in the Americas in 1492?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Estimates of the population of the Americas in 1492 differ by tens of millions. Most surviving tribute lists, parish registers and colonial inspections counted people after epidemics and displacement had begun. Published settlement surveys and radiocarbon dates offer a partly independent record of where people lived, with uneven coverage across regions.
expandedQuestions.method: Reconstruct regions separately. Where early counts and archaeological surveys overlap, test the household sizes and rates of population loss needed to reconcile them. Carry those ranges into the hemispheric total and show which regions dominate the uncertainty. A well-documented valley can anchor its own estimate more securely than its neighbours’.

expandedQuestions.title: By what route did knowledge of gunpowder reach Latin Europe in the thirteenth century?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Chinese texts attest knowledge of gunpowder by the eleventh century. Arabic and Latin references appear in the later thirteenth century, but the route connecting those written traditions remains unclear. Library records, digitized manuscripts and translations preserve names, marginal notes and sometimes a copyist’s date. An author’s purported lifetime can be much earlier than the surviving copy.
expandedQuestions.method: Trace distinctive borrowed terms, named authorities and translation errors across dated witnesses. Look for an inventory, letter or ownership note placing a text with a particular intermediary before the Latin reference appeared. Shared terminology can support contact, but direction and timing need independent documentary evidence.

expandedQuestions.title: What do the thousands of unread Shang oracle-bone graphs mean?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Shang diviners recorded questions and outcomes on bones and turtle shells. Scholars can read many recurring signs, but thousands of distinct forms lack agreed readings. Photographs, ink rubbings and indexed inscriptions are available. A sign may occur only once or only in a personal name, and different hands can write the same word differently.
expandedQuestions.method: Group uncertain signs by their appearance and by the words around them. Propose a reading using one group of inscriptions, then check whether it predicts the sense and grammatical position in previously withheld examples. Compare the original images before counting two drawings as separate evidence.

expandedQuestions.title: How did smallpox reach Aboriginal communities around Sydney in 1789?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Smallpox devastated Aboriginal communities around Sydney in 1789, a year after the British colony was founded. Explanations include an introduction associated with the colony and a much longer route through northern Australia. Dutch records document smallpox at Makassar in 1782 and elsewhere in island Southeast Asia that decade. The intervening chain of cases is missing.
expandedQuestions.method: Read dated Dutch reports alongside Sydney journals and early accounts from inland communities. Establish where each writer actually observed illness and when news reached the writer. An earlier outbreak overseas establishes a possibility. Connecting it to Sydney would require independent evidence along the proposed route.

expandedQuestions.title: Did Europe’s three great medieval cattle plagues come from the east?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Medieval chronicles describe widespread cattle deaths in Europe in 809–810, 937–942 and 1315–1325. Some writers specify cattle, others mention livestock in general, and some describe a severe winter. Digitized Latin, Irish and Arabic texts make it possible to compare reports from different places. Several chronicles can repeat one writer’s account and create the appearance of a much wider event.
expandedQuestions.method: For each episode, trace reports back to their earliest witnesses and record the place, date range and animals named. Map the independent observations and check which regions had chroniclers reporting other livestock losses at the time. The first surviving mention can reflect record keeping as well as geography.

expandedQuestions.title: Were Mendel's pea-hybrid data too close to expectation, and if so, why?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Gregor Mendel published counts of pea plants that closely fit the ratios predicted by his account of inheritance. Ronald Fisher later argued that the overall fit was unusually good. The tables survive, but few working records show how ambiguous plants were classified, experiments repeated or results selected for publication. Different practices could produce similar totals.
expandedQuestions.method: Reconstruct the sequence of experiments from Mendel’s paper and simulate the results of specific counting or reporting practices documented in contemporary sources. Test whether one explanation accounts for several features of the tables at once. Statistical fit can establish plausibility more readily than it can establish someone’s intent.

expandedQuestions.title: Was rongorongo an independent invention of writing?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Roughly two dozen surviving objects from Rapa Nui bear signs known as rongorongo. The inscriptions remain undeciphered. Photographs, transcriptions, three-dimensional scans of some tablets and published dates for their wood are available. Whether people carved the signs before European contact matters to the case for an independent invention of writing.
expandedQuestions.method: Trace each object to its earliest documented appearance and compare repeated passages across tablets. Ask which clues date the carving itself. An old piece of wood could have been inscribed much later, and a regular sequence of signs alone does not establish that it encoded spoken words.

expandedQuestions.title: How did Gutenberg cast his type?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Early printed letters that look identical to the eye show small differences when enlarged. Scholars disagree about whether these variations reveal how Gutenberg made his metal type. High-resolution images of early Mainz printing and several copies of the same Bible pages survive. Ink, paper, pressure and wear can all change the outline left by the same piece of type.
expandedQuestions.method: Compare one letter in the same position across several copies of a page to measure variation introduced during printing. Then compare letters from different positions. Look for features that persist across impressions and check which proposed casting methods could produce the remaining differences.

expandedQuestions.title: How many people were carried in the Indian Ocean slave trades, 1500–1850?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Historians have reconstructed parts of the trade in enslaved people across the Indian Ocean, particularly voyages recorded by European companies. Dutch, Cape and some Portuguese and French records survive online. People also travelled in small groups aboard mixed cargo vessels or with local carriers whose records survive unevenly. The size of these gaps matters to any total.
expandedQuestions.method: Link departures and arrivals using vessel, captain, date and ports. Distinguish repeated reports of the same passage from a later resale or onward voyage. Calculate documented minimums by route and decade, then test how far independent port records support an estimate for missing traffic.

expandedQuestions.title: Did Kerala-school infinite series reach early modern Europe through Jesuit missionaries?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Mathematicians in Kerala developed infinite series for quantities such as π before similar results appeared in seventeenth-century Europe. Jesuits worked in the region and corresponded with European mathematicians. A route for contact is plausible, but no known document records the transfer of those series. Access to manuscript correspondence and Indian mathematical texts varies.
expandedQuestions.method: Search available letters, teaching notes and inventories for a recognizable worked example, diagram or sequence of terms. Date each witness and trace who could have read it before the European discoveries. Parallel mathematical results and travel between the two regions establish different parts of the case.

expandedQuestions.title: Do the missing voices of Renaissance songs survive in lute arrangements?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Renaissance printers often sold each voice of a song in a separate book. A tenor book from a 1536 collection survives in Bern, but some companion parts are missing. Lute players arranged songs so that one instrument could play several voices. Digitized partbooks, lute music and contemporary catalogues allow comparisons even when titles have changed.
expandedQuestions.method: Search lute arrangements for several distinctive phrases of the surviving tenor in the right order. Compare the full pieces, then check how the same arranger treated songs whose vocal parts all survive. An arrangement can recover a historical way to hear the piece while leaving particular lost notes uncertain.

expandedQuestions.title: Which Atlantic shipments can be linked to Europe’s first potato blight outbreaks?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Potato blight appeared in European fields in the 1840s and helped precipitate the Irish famine. Agricultural letters describe early damaged crops, while shipping notices and customs records list consignments of potatoes. A port of departure says little about where a cargo was grown, and a newspaper’s publication date can postdate the first field damage.
expandedQuestions.method: Work backwards from a named grower and a dated report of damage in West Flanders. Look for a purchase, delivery or consignment that can be traced to a particular Atlantic voyage. State where the documents actually connect the shipment to the farm and where the connection remains conjectural.

expandedQuestions.title: Who supplied the medical knowledge that Hans Sloane's catalogues attribute to unnamed people?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Hans Sloane’s medical and botanical collections preserve information from people whose names his catalogues often omit. A European intermediary might be named even when someone else supplied the specimen or explained its use. Digitized catalogue transcriptions, surviving labels and correspondence sometimes describe the same acquisition from different sides.
expandedQuestions.method: Start with an entry that gives a place, approximate date and named intermediary. Follow that person through letters, ship records or accounts for someone described independently in the same transaction. Check whether the evidence identifies the collector, the person who supplied the knowledge, or both.

expandedQuestions.title: Do khipus record more than numbers, and can their non-numerical signs be read?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Andean record keepers tied knots in cords to represent numbers in a decimal system. Colour, the way threads were twisted and the arrangement of pendant cords may also identify people or categories. Public databases record these features, but few khipus can be securely linked to written accounts describing the same community or transaction.
expandedQuestions.method: Start with well-documented pairs of cords and accounts. Propose what a repeated colour or construction feature marks, then predict its use in a different record before reading the associated account. Check whether totals or grouping alone explain the pattern. Reading a category would still leave broader claims about narrative open.

expandedQuestions.title: Which Hittite tablet fragments belong to the same tablet or preserve the same text?
expandedQuestions.evidence: Hittite scribes copied treaties, rituals and other texts onto clay tablets. Many survive in pieces. Searches of the TLHdig sign transcriptions can find plausible continuations, and splitting known texts into artificial fragments has helped test the method. Real pieces are damaged, photographs cover only part of the collection, and two tablets can preserve separate copies of the same passage.
